explanations.explanation: God Himself, friend. The writer says, “so my soul longs after You, O God” (Psalm 42:1). The deer is just the picture. A deer at a stream isn't window shopping, it knows exactly what it came for, and so does he.

Rain would make a deer happy, but this psalm never mentions it. The deer pants “for streams of water,” and then the writer turns the picture on himself: “so my soul longs after You, O God” (Psalm 42:1). The water is the picture. What he longs for is God Himself.
Nobody in this verse is asking for more years. The writer says his soul “longs after You, O God” (Psalm 42:1). He isn't asking for extra pages on the calendar. He wants God Himself.
Not quite. He asks, “When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?” (Psalm 42:2). Somebody who asks “when” isn't there yet. Nobody texts “when will I get to the party” from the middle of the party.

Right, he isn't there yet. He asks, “When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?” (Psalm 42:2). That's a question about getting there. You don't ask the person sitting next to you when they're arriving.
That's the one. Men ask him, “Where is your God?” all day long (Psalm 42:3). I think that question lands heavy on him. It shows up again in verse 10, so it's clearly stuck in his mind.

Nobody in the verse asks about the tears. The men ask him, “Where is your God?” (Psalm 42:3). One question, on repeat, all day long. It's like the coworker who pokes his head in with “got a sec?” for the ninth time.

There's no accusation like that here. The question is “Where is your God?” (Psalm 42:3), and the psalm doesn't say why they ask it. I think it would wear on anybody to hear it all day long. His tears keep coming both day and night, and the question keeps coming too.

explanations.answer: Full of shouts of joy and praise
explanations.explanation: Yes, and it was LOUD. He remembers “leading the festive procession to the house of God with shouts of joy and praise” (Psalm 42:4). That's a parade, friend, and he's at the front of it. I think a memory that happy is exactly why the day he's in now feels so heavy.

His unease shows up in verse 5, but the memory itself is loud. He remembers “the festive procession to the house of God with shouts of joy and praise” (Psalm 42:4). Nobody leads a festive procession on tiptoe. I think the loud memory next to his tears today is what makes this verse sting.

The weeping is the present, in verse 3: “My tears have been my food both day and night.” The memory in verse 4 is of “shouts of joy and praise” (Psalm 42:4). A festive procession at a slow weeping pace would be the saddest parade ever. This one was a celebration.

Hope! He tells his soul, “Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him for the salvation of His presence” (Psalm 42:5). He's a coach at halftime, except the player he's coaching is himself. I think that little word “yet” carries a lot.

Fear isn't what he hands his soul. He says, “Put your hope in God” (Psalm 42:5). His soul is already downcast, and I think he's pointing it somewhere new. A good coach at halftime says “believe,” not “panic.”

He never tells his soul to feel shame. The words are “Put your hope in God” (Psalm 42:5). He asks his soul a question and then hands it an answer. A pep talk that says “feel ashamed” is just another rough day with a microphone.

He remembers. He tells God, “my soul despairs within me. Therefore I remember You from the land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon” (Psalm 42:6). Despair on one side of that line and remembering on the other. I think that's a big deal.

Despair is in the verse, but doubt isn't. He says, “my soul despairs within me,” and then, “Therefore I remember You” (Psalm 42:6). He's still talking to God, calling Him “O my God.” That's a man in despair who keeps the conversation going.

Leaving is hard to pull off while you're still saying “O my God” to Him (Psalm 42:6). He says “my soul despairs within me,” and then, “Therefore I remember You.” The despair is there, but he doesn't walk out. That's like quitting a job while still answering the boss's calls at midnight.

True. He says, “Deep calls to deep in the roar of Your waterfalls; all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me” (Psalm 42:7). See that word “Your”? Ever stand in the ocean for one wave and get three in a row? He's feeling the whole pile of them.

The verse says otherwise. He says “Your waterfalls” and “all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me” (Psalm 42:7). That word “Your” is right there. I'll leave it at what he says, and I think he's feeling the full weight of it.

A song! He says, “at night His song is with me as a prayer to the God of my life” (Psalm 42:8). Right after all those waves in verse 7, here comes a song. I think that's a sweet turn. Loving devotion by day, a song at night.

The psalm doesn't put a heavy silence there. The verse says, “at night His song is with me as a prayer to the God of my life” (Psalm 42:8). After the waves in verse 7, silence might have fit. Instead the verse gives him a song.
A dream sounds cozy, but the verse says “His song” (Psalm 42:8). It's with him “as a prayer to the God of my life.” Sleep isn't mentioned at all. No dreams and no snooze button, just a song at night.

Forgotten. He says to “God my Rock,” “Why have You forgotten me?” (Psalm 42:9). He asks it straight to God, and he calls Him Rock in the very same breath. I think that shows a hard question can be brought right to God.

Chosen would be a nice thing to ask about, but it isn't what he says. His question to God his Rock is “Why have You forgotten me?” (Psalm 42:9). It's a hard one. I think it took courage to say it out loud.
He doesn't say tested. He says, “Why have You forgotten me?” (Psalm 42:9). I think that's a hurting question. He asks it while still calling God “my Rock.”

My Savior and my God! He says, “Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God” (Psalm 42:11). Back in verse 5 that line ended with “for the salvation of His presence,” so check out the new ending. Same line, new words for God. I think each time around he's leaning in a little closer.

A song does show up in verse 8 (Psalm 42:8), but it isn't a name for God here. This line ends with “my Savior and my God” (Psalm 42:11). Shield isn't in the verse at all. Nice titles, but they aren't the ones he uses.

Strong titles, but this verse doesn't use them. He says, “Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God” (Psalm 42:11). Savior and God are the pair. It's like reaching for chocolate chips when the recipe says butterscotch bits.

Deceitful and unjust men. He says, “deliver me from deceitful and unjust men” (Psalm 43:1). Right before that, he asks God to plead his case against “an ungodly nation.” He's asking God to rescue him from people who lie and play unfair.

Rulers don't show up in this verse. He asks God to plead his case against “an ungodly nation” and to “deliver me from deceitful and unjust men” (Psalm 43:1). The words proud and violent aren't there. Those are the exact people he names.
Friends aren't in this verse. He asks God to “deliver me from deceitful and unjust men” (Psalm 43:1). Idle friends sound like a group chat that never makes a plan, but that's a different problem.

The God of my refuge. He says, “For You are the God of my refuge. Why have You rejected me?” (Psalm 43:2). Refuge comes first and the hard question comes second. Both come out in the same breath. I think that's honest.
Fathers isn't the word here. He says, “For You are the God of my refuge” (Psalm 43:2), and then comes his question, “Why have You rejected me?” The word is refuge, and it's personal. It's MY refuge.

The heavens are big, but this verse gets personal. He says, “For You are the God of my refuge” (Psalm 43:2), right before asking, “Why have You rejected me?” The word is refuge, not heavens. I think that small word “my” is doing a lot of work.

explanations.answer: Lead him to where God dwells
explanations.explanation: Lead him to where God dwells. He asks, “Send out Your light and Your truth; let them lead me. Let them bring me to Your holy mountain and to the place where You dwell” (Psalm 43:3). Light and truth are the tour guides, and the destination is God's own place. I think a guide like that never says “recalculating.”
The light isn't aimed at his enemies. He says, “let them lead me” (Psalm 43:3). They're meant to lead HIM. A spotlight on the enemies would be dramatic, but that's not the request.

He doesn't ask for light to expose his sins. He says, “let them lead me. Let them bring me to Your holy mountain” (Psalm 43:3). Light and truth are on guide duty here, not inspection duty. The request is to be led to the place where God dwells.
Joy! The verse says, “to God, my greatest joy” (Psalm 43:4). Not a joy, not a nice joy, the GREATEST. I think he says that with his whole chest.
Burden isn't in the verse. He says God is “my greatest joy” (Psalm 43:4). That's about as far from a burden as you can get. It points in the opposite direction.
Mystery doesn't appear here. He says, “to God, my greatest joy” (Psalm 43:4). He's talking about going to the altar of God. I think he's heading there happy.
Not silent. He says, “Then I will go to the altar of God,” and then, “I will praise You” (Psalm 43:4). Praise isn't a hands-in-the-lap moment. I bet this man plans to make some noise.
False, friend. After he goes to the altar, he says, “I will praise You” (Psalm 43:4). There's no silent treatment planned. A man with a plan to praise isn't planning to be a statue.
The harp! He says, “I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God” (Psalm 43:4). One instrument, no band, no backup singers. I think that sounds beautiful.
A trumpet is a big sound, but the verse names the harp: “I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God” (Psalm 43:4). Trumpets don't appear here. Save the loud brass for another day.
A tambourine would make it a party, but verse 4 says, “I will praise You with the harp” (Psalm 43:4). The harp is the instrument he names. I'd shake a tambourine anyway, but the harp is his pick.
